details.title: Multi-Goal Proof Program Generation with Cache Constraints
Anonymous Evaluator Calibration under RAG Interventions
details.description:
Overview Anonymous Evaluator Calibration under RAG Interventions is a meta-evaluation challenge about predicting how an evaluation system behaves when a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline changes. The model is not given a conventional question-answering benchmark. It is not asked to generate an answer or reproduce a named RAG metric. Every case contains a structured family of alternative answers produced for one latent information need under controlled retrieval and prompting interventions. Each case contains: 32 pipeline variants; one generated answer from every variant; scores from three anonymous evaluator panels; ten anonymous evaluator channels per panel; structured descriptions of the interventions; eight variants with public reference-score calibration labels. The remaining 24 reference scores are hidden and must be predicted. The central question is: given anonymous evaluator behavior on a structured intervention family, can a model predict which pipeline changes improve or degrade the hidden reference assessment? Ephemeral Evaluator Channels The ten evaluator channels do not have stable participant-visible names. Inside every case, the ten channels are independently permuted. A channel exposed as metric_3 in one case may represent a completely different latent criterion in another case. The permutation is shared across the three panels inside one case. Consequently, panel_0.metric_3, panel_1.metric_3, and panel_2.metric_3 refer to the same anonymous criterion within that case. Across cases, metric_3 has no permanent semantic meaning. Participants cannot solve the benchmark by attaching a permanent interpretation or fixed weight to a public metric position. The temporary role of each channel must be inferred from its behavior and the sparse support labels. Ephemeral Evaluator Panels The three panels are represented by temporary case-local positions panel_0, panel_1, and panel_2. Their order is independently permuted in every case. A participant therefore cannot attach one permanent calibration curve to panel_0. Channel permutations and panel permutations are independent. The task is behavioral system identification rather than memorization of named evaluator personalities. Pipeline Variants Every case contains exactly 32 answer variants generated for one underlying information need. Participant-visible intervention metadata includes: a case-local retrieval-family code; retrieval depth; whether full retrieval is used; whether reranking is enabled; a case-local prompt-mode code; whether evidence order was deliberately perturbed. Categorical codes are permuted independently per case. For example, retrieval_code=2 has no universal meaning outside its case. Depth and Boolean intervention fields remain directly interpretable. Answer Text All 32 generated answer texts are public. Original questions, retrieved documents, source evidence, and original gold answers are not public. This is not conventional factual verification. Models must reason from answer behavior, evaluator patterns, intervention structure, and case-local calibration probes. Answer text may expose surface and semantic signals, but it does not directly contain the hidden reference score. Evaluator Tensor Each case contains an evaluator tensor with shape [32,3,10]: 32 pipeline variants; 3 anonymous panels; 10 anonymous metric channels. The tensor contains ordinary evaluator outputs. The hidden reference signal is not included in the tensor. Evaluator calls may occasionally fail. A matching Boolean validity tensor identifies which values are valid. Invalid cells contain a neutral serialization placeholder and must be masked or imputed by the participant. Hidden Reference Score Every pipeline variant has one scalar reference score $y\in[0,1]$. The reference is constructed from a held-out evaluation signal that is not one of the ten public metric channels. It is the target of the benchmark, not a claim that an automated evaluator is equivalent to objective truth. Case-Local Calibration Every case contains exactly eight support variants. Their reference scores are public inside the case file. The remaining 24 variants are targets. Support variants never appear as submission targets for that case. Evaluator panels, metric positions, retrieval codes, and prompt codes are re-randomized for each case. The eight supports therefore provide case-local evidence about which anonymous behaviors are predictive. Eight probes cover several intervention regions but do not label every configuration. A model must generalize across the structured variant family. Target Anchors Every target variant has one public support anchor identified by anchor_variant_ids. The anchor is selected as a nearby support variant in intervention space. Its reference score is already public through support_reference_scores. For target $i$, the model must estimate both: the absolute hidden reference level $y_i$; the response $\delta_i=y_i-y_{a(i)}$ relative to its calibrated anchor. Large true anchor-relative changes receive moderately greater evaluator weight than nearly neutral changes. This makes intervention response a real scoring component rather than a duplicate label attached to ordinary squared error. Public Files The public package contains: train.csv; test.csv; train_targets.csv; sample_submission.csv; cases/; metadata/task_config.json. There is no provided development split. Case Index Files train.csv and test.csv each contain one row per case. Their columns are exactly: case_key; case_path; group_id. case_key is an opaque public case-row identifier. case_path points to the corresponding compressed NumPy case file. group_id is an opaque evaluation-condition grouping key for grouped validation. The case index deliberately does not contain case_id, variant_id, id, or reference_score. Those names belong to the prediction contract and do not appear as public test feature columns. Case Files Every .npz file under cases/ contains: schema_version, shape [1]; case_key, shape [1]; variant_ids, shape [32]; answer_texts, shape [32]; metric_scores, shape [32,3,10]; metric_valid, shape [32,3,10]; support_mask, shape [32]; support_reference_scores, shape [32]; anchor_variant_ids, shape [32]; retrieval_code, shape [32]; retrieval_depth, shape [32]; full_retrieval, shape [32]; rerank, shape [32]; prompt_code, shape [32]; shuffled, shape [32]. Values in support_reference_scores are meaningful only where support_mask is true. anchor_variant_ids is populated for target variants and blank for supports. The case files do not contain permanent evaluator names, permanent metric names, original source identifiers, hidden target reference scores, source questions, retrieved contexts, or gold answers. Training Targets train_targets.csv contains one row for every non-support target variant in every training case. Its columns are: id; case_id; variant_id; reference_score. id is globally unique. case_id equals the corresponding case file's public case_key. Each reference score lies in [0,1]. Train and Test Separation The official split satisfies two simultaneous holdouts. Composition Holdout Each evaluation group represents a dataset–generator composition that is absent from training. A generator and a dataset may each occur elsewhere in training, but their held-out pairing does not. Source-Family Holdout An underlying information need is assigned wholly away from the opposite split within its dataset. Evaluation information needs do not reappear in training under another generator. Cases that would violate either holdout are excluded rather than reassigned. This prevents answer-text matching across generators from recovering supervision for the same latent information need. For local validation, participants should group by group_id and should keep all variants and derived features from one case together. Submission Format Use sample_submission.csv exactly. Its columns are: id; case_id; variant_id; reference_score. Every id is globally unique. Participants must preserve id, case_id, and variant_id and replace only reference_score. Predictions must be finite numbers in [0,1]. Duplicate IDs, missing IDs, unknown IDs, altered case mappings, altered variant mappings, extra columns, reordered columns, non-finite predictions, and out-of-domain predictions receive the evaluator floor. The private answers.csv begins with exactly the same four columns in the same order and may append private grading fields. Those additional fields must not appear in a submission. Absolute Reference Error For target $i$, let $y_i$ be the hidden reference score and $p_i$ the prediction. The level error is $e_{\mathrm{level},i}=(p_i-y_i)^2$. For one case, $E_{\mathrm{level}}$ is the mean level error over its 24 targets. Intervention-Response Error Let $a(i)$ be target $i$'s public support anchor. The true and predicted intervention responses are $\delta_i=y_i-y_{a(i)}$ and $\hat\delta_i=p_i-y_{a(i)}$. Define intervention importance as $w_i=1+\min(|\delta_i|,1)$. Since reference scores lie in [0,1], $w_i$ lies in [1,2]. The weighted response error is $e_{\mathrm{response},i}=w_i(\hat\delta_i-\delta_i)^2$. For one case, $E_{\mathrm{response}}$ is the mean weighted response error over its 24 targets. Although the unweighted delta residual equals $p_i-y_i$, the public anchor changes the evaluator through $w_i$. Errors on genuinely consequential interventions therefore count more than equally sized errors on nearly neutral interventions. Per-Case Error and Score The total case error is $E_{\mathrm{case}}=0.55E_{\mathrm{level}}+0.45E_{\mathrm{response}}$. Both terms are nonnegative, so $E_{\mathrm{case}}\ge0$. The case score is $s_{\mathrm{case}}=\frac{1}{1+E_{\mathrm{case}}/0.15^2}$. A perfect case has score 1. Increasing finite error strictly decreases the score across the complete prediction domain. The rational kernel is used instead of an exponential kernel so progressively degraded predictions remain distinguishable rather than collapsing into underflow or the evaluator floor. Final Aggregation Case scores are averaged within each private compositional group. The final score is the macro-average across represented groups: $\mathrm{finalscore}=100\times\operatorname{mean}{g}(\operatorname{mean}{c\in g}s_{\mathrm{case},c})$. The result is clipped to [0.01,100]. A perfect submission receives exactly 100. Malformed submissions receive 0.01. Grading is deterministic. There is no LLM judge, external API, embedding service, or manual interpretation at grading time. Baseline Difficulty The public anchors, supports, and evaluator tensor make meaningful statistical baselines possible, but no single field is an answer key. A nearest-support baseline over the anonymous evaluator tensor is expected to sit near the lower edge of the target competitive band. Stronger systems must combine intervention structure, cross-panel disagreement, answer text, and case-local calibration. The intended useful leaderboard region is approximately 50–70 for credible learned baselines. Perfect and near-perfect scores require substantially more accurate calibration rather than exploitation of identifiers or repeated source questions. Modeling Directions A simple model may average panels, derive permutation-invariant statistics, and calibrate against the eight supports. Stronger approaches may use: answer length, refusal, formatting, and citation features; intervention-aware nearest-neighbor regression; regularized case-local regression; panel disagreement and channel variance; pretrained answer-text encoders; permutation-equivariant metric encoders; set transformers; graph neural networks over intervention relationships; neural processes or other few-shot regression models; low-rank evaluator factorization; hierarchical Bayesian calibration; joint text-and-tensor meta-learning. A natural representation treats variants as nodes, anonymous channels as temporary latent factors, and support scores as sparse observations over the case graph. Compute Budget The intended environment provides one NVIDIA A10G-class GPU with approximately 24 GB VRAM and a 90-minute end-to-end runtime budget. The evaluator tensors are small. Most optional compute comes from answer-text encoding. Lightweight statistical calibration, pretrained sentence encoders, and compact joint models are all viable. Remote inference services are not allowed. Allowed Resources Participants may use released challenge files, public pretrained text checkpoints, standard numerical and machine-learning libraries, local feature extraction, and grouped validation derived from public metadata. Disallowed Shortcuts Participants may not use private evaluator files, hidden target labels, original source identifiers, recovered source questions or contexts, external labeled copies of evaluation cases, manual test annotation, hard-coded target values, submission-feedback reconstruction, or identifier and row-order semantics. Matching an evaluation information need to an external or private copy of the source corpus is not allowed. Scope The benchmark evaluates meta-reasoning about anonymous automated evaluation systems. It does not evaluate retrieval execution, generation of new answers, or objective factual truth. The challenge is to decode the temporary jury, understand the intervention family, and predict the hidden reference response from sparse calibration evidence.
Closes in 3h 11m
